name: Femi Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Femi, and thanks for this. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me is confidential and won't have your name on it. So feel free to tell me what you'd say out loud and also what you really think. All right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a pretty straight talker anyway, so it probably won't be that different.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm on the new east wing at Riverside General, doing formwork, which means building the timber and steel moulds that the concrete gets poured into. I'm an improver, so I fetch, carry, cut ply and hold things while Sandra, the chargehand, checks my levels, because my levels still drift. Pour days are the best, everyone's buzzing and the pay's good if it runs late. The worst part is stripping the forms afterwards, prising off wet ply covered in release oil in the rain, and my partner Ama will be working a ward inside that wing one day, which is funny when I think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's a pretty comfortable picture for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, well, there you go, the hype train ran out of track. At work Marek and I would laugh about the guy from the main contractor who kept saying the site would be run by an app. Online I mostly lurk, so maybe I'd just like a few posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means my plan stays my plan. Finish learning formwork properly, get my carpentry card, and in a few years be the one checking someone else's levels. The extra pay from pours and late nights keeps going into savings, and Ama and I buy a flat in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I'm doing. I've got just over a year of wages saved and the car's paid off, so there's no pressure. I'd sign up for the formwork course the company offers in March, which I was going to do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, maybe, because there's always that noise in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's always that noise in the background. What is that noise, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's videos, mostly. Some guy in a hard hat showing a robot laying bricks, a million views, and every comment says builders are finished. I've never seen one of those robots on a real site, but you see it enough times and it gets in your head a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. When we got a new formwork system with instructions in German, I took photos and had one of those chat apps translate them, and it was mostly right. I wouldn't trust it for loads or anything structural, Sandra would kill me.

S0.say: I'd say the hype train ran out of track. At work I'd laugh with Marek about the manager who said the whole site would be run by an app.
S0.think: My plan stays my plan: learn formwork properly, get my carpentry card, and one day check someone else's levels. The pour money keeps going into savings and Ama and I buy a flat in a couple of years.
S0.do: Keeps working as he does now, with just over a year of wages saved and a paid-off car. Signs up in March for the company's formwork course, which he'd planned anyway.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little relieved that the background noise about robots goes quiet.
S0.quote: I wouldn't trust it for loads or anything structural, Sandra would kill me.
S0.fieldNote: Femi is level-headed and already uses AI in small, practical ways, while drawing a clear line at structural safety. The 'noise' he describes comes from online videos, not his own site. His plan is concrete and well funded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture now. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I can see that one. That feels close to what's already happening, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the workers need a seat at the table when these changes come in, and that companies shouldn't get to pocket all the savings. I'd say it to Marek and at the pub, and I'd probably share the union's posts on it. I'm a member, but I don't go to meetings much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think formwork could be one of the bits that changes. There's talk of reusable plastic systems and printed concrete that don't need a lot of us cutting ply. I don't think it takes my job, but it might take the part of the job I'm learning right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what actually shows up on site, because there's a lot of talk that never arrives. Once a couple of the lads are using a new layout app or system and it works, I'd learn it, probably on a weekend with Marek. Meanwhile I'd keep saving like normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, just paying more attention than I used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until a couple of the lads are using something. Why wait, rather than go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen first goes go wrong. Last year they brought in a laser system for checking the forms and it was off by a few millimetres for a week before someone found out the tripod was loose. I'd rather let somebody else find the loose tripod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ama about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're fine, and I'd mean it. She'd probably point out that hospitals are already using AI for rotas and scans, and she'd ask if we should wait on the flat. I'd say no, the flat's still a good idea.

S1.say: I'd say workers need a seat at the table when these changes come in, and companies shouldn't pocket all the savings. I'd share the union's posts even though I rarely go to meetings.
S1.think: Formwork could be one of the bits that changes, with reusable plastic systems and printed concrete. I don't think it takes my job, but it might take the part I'm learning now.
S1.do: Waits to see what new systems actually reach his site before acting. Learns a new tool once a couple of colleagues have proved it works, and keeps saving at his usual pace.
S1.feel: Uneasy, paying closer attention than before but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: I'd rather let somebody else find the loose tripod.
S1.fieldNote: His caution is grounded in a real memory of a new laser system failing for a week. He favours fair sharing of gains but is a passive union member. He sees change as reshaping the job rather than ending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's different. That's the hospital getting finished and then nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in hard, with income support and rules on how fast companies can lay people off. I'd say it online for once, properly, not just likes. And I'd tell everyone on site to join the union, because a deal is better than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd lose my job and so might Ama, maybe a bit later than me. That's the part that gets me, the both of us at once. Having a year of money saved feels good until you realise a year isn't that long if nothing comes back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd go to a union meeting, the first one in ages, and actually stand up. We'd put the flat on hold, no question, and keep the deposit money where we can reach it. I'd cut the takeaways and the gym, and stretch our savings so that between us we've got maybe two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I think I'd still feel like I had my hands on the wheel for a while, because of the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the both of you at once. What would that first conversation with Ama look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kitchen table, probably after one of her late shifts, so tired. I'd have the bank app open and a list on paper. She'd want to talk about her mum and whether we'd need to help her, and I'd want to talk about the flat, and we'd end up talking about both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you usually wait for others to prove something first. With only two years, does that still work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that worries me. If I wait for the lads to go first, the two years are half gone. I'd have to act before anyone has proved anything, and that's not really who I am.

S2.say: I'd say governments need to step in hard, with income support and rules on how fast companies can lay people off. I'd post about it properly and tell everyone on site to join the union.
S2.think: I'd lose my job and Ama might lose hers a bit later, and the two of us at once is what gets me. A year of savings feels good until you realise a year isn't long if nothing comes back.
S2.do: Attends a union meeting for the first time in ages and speaks up. Puts the flat purchase on hold, cuts takeaways and the gym, and stretches the couple's savings to cover about two years.
S2.feel: Anxious, though the savings let him feel he still has his hands on the wheel for a while.
S2.quote: Having a year of money saved feels good until you realise a year isn't that long if nothing comes back.
S2.fieldNote: The shared risk with Ama is what shifts him, not his own job alone. He notices that his habit of waiting for proof doesn't work on a two-year clock. He stays anxious rather than alarmed because of the money and the joint planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd have my carpentry card by then, if I don't mess it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message really, government needs a plan, but I'd add that five years is enough to do this right if they start now. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. I might even write to our local representative, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years is the worst for someone like me, because it's long enough to feel safe and short enough to be wrong. I'd be qualified just in time for it to stop mattering. And my habit of waiting would eat two of the five years without me noticing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set myself a rule: watch for one year, and if I see the robots actually working on a real site, start retraining in year two. I'd look at something on the inspection or safety side, signing off work, because somebody still has to be responsible. And we'd delay the flat by a couple of years and keep building the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a slow kind of anxious. Like checking the forecast every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspection or safety, rather than another trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a robot can pour a wall, but I'm not sure people will let it sign off a hospital wing on its own. At least not at first. There'd still need to be a person whose name is on the paper, and I'd rather be that person than the one holding the ply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that something you know, or something you hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hope, if I'm honest. I don't really know. Nobody does.

S3.say: I'd say government needs a plan and five years is enough to do it right if they start now. I might even write to my local representative for the first time.
S3.think: Five years is the worst for me because it's long enough to feel safe and short enough to be wrong. My habit of waiting could eat two of the five years without me noticing.
S3.do: Gives himself one year to watch for working robots on real sites, then starts retraining in year two towards inspection or safety sign-off. Delays the flat by a couple of years and keeps building savings.
S3.feel: A slow, steady anxiety, like checking the forecast every day.
S3.quote: A robot can pour a wall, but I'm not sure people will let it sign off a hospital wing on its own.
S3.fieldNote: Femi builds a rule to beat his own tendency to wait, which is a thoughtful move. His retraining idea rests on a hope that people will still be needed to take responsibility, and he admits it's a hope. He sees the middle timeline as the most dangerous for someone like him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last picture, ten years. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's enough time for a whole second career, almost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where nobody has an excuse. Governments, companies, unions, all of them can plan. I'd push the union to get retraining money written into every big contract now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one I can work with. Ten years means I can finish formwork, earn well for a few years, buy the flat, and then move into something else once I see where it's heading. By then other people will have tried things and I'll know what actually works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat with Ama, maybe next year, while I'm earning well. I'd get my carpentry card and then, around year four or five, do a course in site inspection or something next to it. And I'd get better with the AI tools, slowly, the way I did with the translation, using them more on the job once they're proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's still there, but it feels like something you can plan around, like a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've moved the flat forward compared to the five-year picture. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years I'd have most of a mortgage term worked before it hits, and Ama's job is probably safer for longer than mine. If it's five years, a flat feels like a weight. If it's ten, it's a place to land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what about the people at work, who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, mostly. He's forty-four, steel fixer, doesn't read English well and won't touch a phone app. Ten years would take him to fifty-four, which is a hard age to start again, and I don't think anyone has a plan for guys like him.

S4.say: I'd say this is the version where nobody has an excuse to skip planning. I'd push the union to get retraining money written into every big contract now.
S4.think: This one I can work with: finish formwork, earn well, buy the flat, then move once I see where it's heading. By then other people will have tried things and I'll know what works.
S4.do: Buys a flat with Ama within about a year while he's earning well, and gets his carpentry card. Plans a site inspection course around year four or five and gradually uses AI tools more on the job once they're proven.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but it feels like something to plan around, like a pension.
S4.quote: If it's five years, a flat feels like a weight. If it's ten, it's a place to land.
S4.fieldNote: The long timeline suits his style exactly: others go first and he follows what works. He reverses his flat decision depending on the warning time, a clear sign of how time changes his choices. His concern for Marek shows he thinks about who gets left out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Ama and I could both be out at once, and I wouldn't have time to do things my way, which is watching first. What would help is a guaranteed income for a few years while people retrain, paid for by the companies making the money, and clear rules that you can't just lay off a whole site overnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the older guys. Everyone asks people my age because we can supposedly adapt. But I've got savings and time. It's the Mareks I'd be asking about.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks people my age because we can supposedly adapt. But I've got savings and time. It's the Mareks I'd be asking about.
portrait: Femi Zhang is a 27-year-old formwork improver on a hospital extension, living with his partner Ama, a nurse, with just over a year of wages saved and a flat in their plans. He's calm, practical and progressive, and uses AI now and then but waits for others to prove new tools first. In the mild pictures he keeps to his plan, while the fast AGI picture makes him anxious because he and Ama could lose work together and he'd have no time to watch before acting. The longer timelines let him plan a move into inspection work, and he keeps thinking of older colleagues like Marek who would struggle most.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he and Ama could both lose work at once and he wouldn't have time to watch others before acting.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income for a few years while people retrain, paid for by the companies profiting, plus rules against laying off a whole site overnight.
